name: WeavePy
workload: 24 in-repo Python benchmark fixtures (deltablue, richards, nbody, fannkuch, fib, spectral_norm, json_bench, pickle_bench, pidigits, etc.) plus a startup fixture, run by the weavepy-bench gate; per-fixture median of the fixture's own timer, interleaved with CPython on the same machine.
claimed_speedup: Geometric mean over the 24 fixtures is 0.50 of CPython's time (about 2x faster, derived from page data); sumvm 0.05x, jitloop and nested_loops 0.08x, spectral_norm 0.20x, fib 0.36x, richards 0.55x, startup 0.79x; but slower than CPython on deltablue (3.03x CPython time), generators (1.10x) and dict_ops (1.06x). PR #82 reported 0.59x geomean over 23 fixtures.
compiler_and_flags: Rust release profile (opt-level 3, fat LTO, codegen-units 1 per Cargo.toml) with profile-guided build via tools/pgo_build.py (-Cprofile-generate/-Cprofile-use); JIT on
hardware: macOS x86-64 development host, Intel Core i9-9980HK
tradeoffs: Python interpreter written in Rust aiming at drop-in CPython 3.14 compatibility, but compatibility is still partial (README tracks conformance against CPython's own test suite); the report says importing large stdlib modules still costs about 2x CPython and peak memory after those imports is about 2x. Needs a Rust toolchain; native JIT tiers.
caveats: Own benchmark harness and fixtures (ported pyperformance-style programs), one development laptop; the CPython 3.14.8 build and its flags are not stated, so the baseline may not be a PGO/LTO build. The doc is a work-in-progress branch report ('works toward making WeavePy faster than CPython on every fixture'), committed baselines in the README moved between releases, and the headline geomean is dominated by JIT-friendly loop kernels (sumvm, jitloop, nested_loops at 0.05-0.08x). Very new project with 3 stars; fixtures with ratios above 1 are slower than CPython.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust Python interpreter faster than CPython benchmark startup github' surfaced PR #82 (weavefoundry/weavepy); then opened docs/PERFORMANCE-CPYTHON-PARITY.md, tools/pgo_build.py and Cargo.toml

name: Wangshu (望舒)
baseline: gopher-lua v1.1.2 (pure-Go Lua 5.1 VM); PUC Lua 5.1.5 is used only as a correctness oracle, not as a timing baseline
workload: Go benchmarks run with -benchtime=2s -count=3 -cpu=1 (median): micro benchmarks (branch, Horner arithmetic, sum loop), heavy numeric kernels (HeavyArith, HeavyRecursion, HeavyFloatloop) and small real programs (fib, binary-trees, spectral-norm, fannkuch, n-body), on three platforms in the same CI run.
claimed_speedup: Linux/amd64 vs gopher-lua: P4 method JIT 18.0-18.5x on HeavyArith and HeavyFloatloop, 15.4x on spectral-norm, 14.7x on n-body, 9.35x on fib, 7.87x on fannkuch, 1.89x on binary-trees; the plain P1 interpreter is 1.27-5.54x faster on the micro, heavy and most small-program rows but slower than gopher-lua on fib (0.87x) and fannkuch (0.77x).
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain per go.mod; go test benchmark flags -benchtime=2s -count=3 -cpu=1, median of 3; benchmark script scripts/bench-readme-table.sh, CI workflow bench-readme-table (run 29098511106, 2026-07-10)
hardware: GitHub Actions hosted runners: Linux/amd64 Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, Linux/arm64 Azure Cobalt 100, macOS arm64 (Apple M-series)
tradeoffs: Pure Go, no cgo; implements only Lua 5.1 core (no io.open/popen/tmpfile, partial debug library, VARARG stays on the interpreter path); the fast tiers (P3 Wasm compile layer, P4 method JIT) are release-candidate state and a trace JIT (P5) is not implemented. Binary-compatible output with Lua 5.1.5 is checked by differential fuzzing.
caveats: Baseline is gopher-lua (itself roughly 3x slower than C Lua per its own wiki), so the ratios say little about PUC Lua 5.4 or LuaJIT; there is no direct PUC Lua timing in the table. Hosted runners are shared VMs, the README itself says wall time drifts 10-20% between runs and ratios should be used. Some rows lose to gopher-lua (fib 0.87x, fannkuch 0.77x on P1). README is primarily Chinese (README.en.md exists, not opened). Project is new with 8 stars.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/lua-vm (description claims 'Up to 17x faster than gopher-lua on numeric kernels'); then opened README.md

name: jaq
workload: 30 jq-filter benchmarks run by bench.sh: startup (empty filter x512), a Brainfuck interpreter written in jq (bf-fib), sort, group-by, reverse, min-max, add on 1,048,576 elements, object and tree updates, to-fromjson on 65,536, ack, cumsum, str-slice.
claimed_speedup: jaq-3.0 is fastest on 20 of the benchmarks, jq-1.8.1 on 5, gojq on 6; e.g. sort 90 ms vs 430 ms, group-by 260 vs 1790 ms, to-fromjson 50 vs 350 ms, tree-contains 90 vs 830 ms, bf-fib 530 vs 1030 ms; jq wins reduce (700 vs 740 ms), pyramid (250 vs 300), ack (490 vs 570), cumsum-xy (350 vs 380); startup 410 vs 430 ms per 512 runs.
compiler_and_flags: jaq built with cargo build --release; jq-1.8.1 from the official Arch Linux package, gojq-0.12.18 from its GitHub release binary; timing via /usr/bin/time -f %U in bench.sh (10 s timeout per run)
hardware: Linux system with an AMD Ryzen 5 5500U
tradeoffs: Reimplementation of the jq language in Rust with its own differences (stricter handling of some jq quirks); not every jq feature or CLI option is identical. Binary or crate usable from Rust.
caveats: Author-run benchmarks on one laptop CPU; times are user CPU seconds not wall time; baseline jq is a distro build whose flags are not stated; gojq is much faster on tree-flatten (native flatten) and wins several rows, and jq wins 5, so the claim is 'faster on most', not all. jq is a filter language interpreter, not one of the listed baselines.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/01mf02/jaq while checking jq-clone interpreters; read README Performance section and bench.sh

name: frawk
baseline: gawk 5.1 (Linux) / 5.0.1 (macOS) and mawk 1.3.4, run with gawk -b
workload: AWK-style CSV and TSV processing on 5.2 GB HEPMASS all_train and 8.9 GB TREE_GRM_ESTN files: sum two columns, statistics, select, filter, group by key.
claimed_speedup: Sum two columns, macOS configuration, all_train TSV: gawk 10.4 s and mawk 10.8 s vs frawk (LLVM) 3.1 s and parallel frawk 1.7 s; TREE_GRM_ESTN TSV: gawk 14.0 s, mawk 42.0 s vs frawk 10.0 s / parallel 3.4 s. Linux configuration: gawk 23.1 s vs frawk 14.7 s on TREE_GRM_ESTN TSV. The doc says on a per-core basis frawk beats mawk and gawk but is slower than tsv-utils. Group By Key is a tie with gawk (14.8 s vs 14.8 s on macOS).
compiler_and_flags: frawk built with use_jemalloc and allow_avx2 features, LLVM and Cranelift backends 'with all optimizations enabled'; mawk on Linux compiled from source with -march=native; gawk invoked with -b; rustc/LLVM versions not stated
hardware: macOS: 16-inch MacBook Pro with 8-core i9 2.3 GHz (boost 4.8 GHz); Linux: dual-socket workstation with 2 x 8-core Xeon E5-2620v4 2.2 GHz, 64 GB RAM, Ubuntu 18.04
tradeoffs: AWK dialect with its own semantics (explicit numeric conversion needed in comparisons, CSV/TSV input modes), parallel mode splits input across workers; build needs LLVM or uses Cranelift; maintainer says bug-fix time is limited.
caveats: Author's own benchmarks, scripts are in info/scripts but compiler versions are missing and the numbers date from about 2021; frawk is slower than gawk or tied on some workloads (Group By Key) and slower than tsv-utils everywhere per-core; the doc itself asks readers to draw only modest conclusions. gawk and mawk are AWK implementations, not one of the listed category baselines.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/ezrosent/frawk while checking AWK and jq-style language interpreters; read info/performance.md

name: sjsonnet
workload: Evaluating one large production Jsonnet config (staging/runbot-app.jsonnet in the Databricks codebase, about 6.6 MB of output).
claimed_speedup: Sjsonnet 0.4.3 about 0.10 s vs go-jsonnet 0.20.0 about 6.5 s vs google/jsonnet 0.20.0 about 67 s (about 65x vs go-jsonnet and 670x vs google/jsonnet, derived from page data); README dated May 18, 2023.
tradeoffs: JVM implementation of the Jsonnet language (Scala); best when kept as a warm long-lived process; startup cost of a cold JVM applies for one-shot use.
caveats: The measured file is internal to Databricks and not reproducible; the README says Sjsonnet was run as a long-lived daemon to keep the JVM warm while go-jsonnet and google/jsonnet were run as subprocesses (process start included), so the ratio is not like for like. No hardware, JVM version or flags stated; single data point from 2023. The Databricks 2018 blog post 'Writing a Faster Jsonnet Compiler' is referenced but was not opened.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/databricks/sjsonnet while checking Jsonnet implementations

name: Tengo
baseline: GopherLua (Lua 5.1 VM in Go), go-lua, goja, starlark-go, gpython, Yaegi, otto, Anko; native Lua and Python 2 listed as reference rows
workload: Recursive fib(35) and tail-call fibt(35) executed by each embeddable Go scripting language.
claimed_speedup: fib(35): Tengo 2,315 ms vs go-lua 4,028 ms, GopherLua 4,409 ms, goja 5,194 ms, starlark-go 6,954 ms, gpython 11,324 ms, Yaegi 11,715 ms, otto 48,539 ms, Anko 52,821 ms; fibt(35): Tengo 3 ms vs Yaegi 10 ms.
tradeoffs: Statically-bytecode-compiled dynamic scripting language with its own syntax (not Lua, Python or JavaScript); pure Go, no cgo, sandbox-friendly.
caveats: Single recursive microbenchmark in the project's own README; hardware, Go version and flags are not stated; the code lives in a separate repo (d5/tengobench) that was not opened. The same README table shows native Lua 5.x at 756 ms and native Python 2 at 1,907 ms, both faster than Tengo (2,315 ms), so Tengo beats other Go-hosted interpreters, not the C implementations of CPython or Lua.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/d5/tengo after the GitHub scripting-language topic page and a search for Go scripting engines

name: GopherLua
baseline: CPython 3.4.3 (also C Lua 5.1.4, go-lua, otto, anko)
workload: Recursive fib(35) (result 9,227,465) timed once per implementation.
claimed_speedup: fib(35): GopherLua 5.40 s vs Python 3.4 5.84 s (about 1.08x faster, derived from page data), vs go-lua 8.13 s, otto 173.32 s, anko 182.73 s; but C Lua 5.1.4 is 1.71 s (about 3.2x faster than GopherLua). README: 'almost equivalent (or little bit better) performance as Python3 on micro benchmarks'.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.7; no flags stated; Lua 5.1.4 and Python 3.4.3
hardware: Windows 7 64-bit, 2 CPUs, 8 GB RAM (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Lua 5.1 VM in pure Go with a Go-friendly (non stack-based) API, goroutine and channel integration; README says it is 'not fast but not too slow'; using Go contexts for cancellation costs about 40% (7.5 s vs 5.3 s in the README example).
caveats: Very old single-benchmark wiki page (Go 1.7, Python 3.4, Windows 7) and the margin over CPython is about 8%; it is about 3x slower than reference C Lua. Included mainly as the baseline for Go-hosted Lua VMs and as a marginal result against CPython.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/yuin/gopher-lua README then the wiki Benchmarks page, after Wangshu and Tengo named it as their baseline

name: goja
workload: Not stated in the README; general JavaScript execution ('on average').
claimed_speedup: README: 'it's 6-7 times faster than otto on average'; the Tengo README's fib(35) table independently shows goja 5,194 ms vs otto 48,539 ms (about 9.3x, derived from that page's data).
tradeoffs: ECMAScript 5.1 plus most of ES6+ in pure Go with no cgo; the README states plainly it is not a replacement for V8 or SpiderMonkey and that cgo-based engines are faster for computation-heavy code.
caveats: The README gives a ratio but no workload, hardware or method; an issue (goja#2) asked for the benchmark code and the maintainer's comment holds only the same sentence. Does not beat V8, QuickJS or any engine in the category baseline list. Baseline otto is itself slow.
found_via: GitHub javascript-engine topic page and WebFetch of github.com/dop251/goja README

name: S6 (DeepMind CPython JIT)
workload: Three public pyperformance benchmarks (richards, raytrace, unpack_sequence) run with S6's JIT enabled in CPython 3.7.
claimed_speedup: Richards: 7x over the default Python 3.7 interpreter at 100 iterations, 9.5x average on internal dev machines; raytrace 3-4.5x; unpack_sequence worst case 0.2x (a 5x slowdown) or 0.97x in a tweaked variant; README headline 'up to 10x over CPython for pure Python benchmarks'.
tradeoffs: Standalone JIT library for CPython 3.7 (strongjit IR lowered to x86 with asmjit); emits x86 machine code via asmjit; calls into C APIs such as NumPy are bottlenecked by C API call time; needs the project's Docker build.
caveats: Archived on 2023-07-05; DeepMind says it stopped work on S6; the README says most testing used internal or private benchmarks and the public numbers are for three benchmarks with minor modifications. Target is CPython 3.7, long out of support. Hardware unspecified. License file is at src/LICENSE (Apache-2.0), not at the repo root. Last commit date was not visible on the repo page (single commit).
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than CPython" github project Python interpreter OR runtime OR compiler' returned github.com/deepmind/s6

name: cperl
baseline: perl5 (version not stated in the claim; also 'more than 2x faster than 5.14')
claimed_speedup: Project description: 'about 15% faster than perl5 overall, more than 2x faster than 5.14'; also claims the least memory measured since perl 5.6.
tradeoffs: Diverged fork of perl5 adding types, classes, native compilation hooks and security hardening while keeping CPAN compatibility; not a drop-in for every perl5 release.
caveats: Claim has no benchmark script, workload, hardware or version on the repo page (the fetch showed the text with a typo '15%x'); archived read-only on 2023-06-01 and the last commit shown is 2022-07-29. Treat as a directional claim with one number.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/perl11/cperl while checking Perl, PHP and R interpreter forks

name: Expr (expr-lang)
baseline: cel-go (also compared against goja, govaluate, otto, gval, starlark-go)
workload: Evaluating one small expression per iteration in each Go expression-evaluation library, go test -bench with 20 s per benchmark (main case plus string matching, function call and map cases).
claimed_speedup: Main benchmark: expr 70.27 ns/op vs cel-go 91.27, goja 146.2, govaluate 152.9, otto 380.1, gval 412.9, evalfilter 990.6, bexpr 1276, starlark 2653 ns/op (expr about 1.3x faster than cel-go, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: go test -bench=. -benchtime=20s; Go version not stated
tradeoffs: Statically typed, side-effect-free expression language compiled to bytecode and run on a stack VM, always terminating; not a general-purpose scripting language.
caveats: The comparison repo is written by Expr's own author and its last commit is August 2023, so versions of the rivals are dated; one tiny expression per iteration says little about larger programs. The category baselines (CPython, Lua, MRI, V8) are not involved; goja and otto stand in for JavaScript engines and are Go-hosted. The Expr README itself only links to the comparison.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/expr-lang/expr README (links its benchmarks), then github.com/antonmedv/golang-expression-evaluation-comparison

name: GoAWK
baseline: awk (one-true-awk) and gawk; mawk is faster than GoAWK
workload: AWK script execution on GoAWK's bytecode compiler and virtual machine; the README links an article with the benchmark results (not opened).
claimed_speedup: README: 'Most AWK scripts are faster than awk and on a par with gawk, though usually slower than mawk.' No numbers on the repo page.
tradeoffs: AWK interpreter in Go with CSV/TSV support and a Go API for embedding; regular-expression heavy scripts are slower than other implementations because Go's regexp is slow (README).
caveats: Tier D: the numbers are in a blog article (benhoyt.com, linked from the README as 'goawk-compiler-vm') that is blocked in this environment and was not opened. The claim itself concedes mawk is usually faster. Kept as the single tier D entry because of its notability.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/benhoyt/goawk while checking AWK and jq-style interpreters
